doc.title: Willie J. Humphrey and Willie E. Humphrey Interview, 1959-03-15
doc.interviewee: Willie J. Humphrey and Willie E. Humphrey

title: Frankie Dusen: his roughness, a broken horn and the smashed bass
summary: Stories about Frankie Dusen's playing, a replacement horn, and a drunk who broke Alex Scott's bass at the Boston club.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: How was Frankie in those days? Was he pretty rough, or was he smooth playing, or how was he doing?
Rough. Rough as they made him. Really? We had a father now, he would've. He begged me, begged me to come back with him, but I never would go back and play with him. Was he rough?
Oh yeah, you know he was fly. Frankie Duesen was a chur.

Frankie Duesen told me at the time they played at the old Paris Prism and he was playing the valve I believe, I don't know if it was valve or slide, I don't know what it was, but anyway, one of them keepers broke his horn, or somebody broke his horn. Broke Frank his horn, yeah. Yeah. So he said, I'm sorry, I don't worry about it, I'll buy you another. So Frank was kind of glad, you know. So he made him go to the oil lines, or glue walls, I believe it was. And the old man that was the clerk there, and his man met him. So the horns were cheaper than what they are now, but the man thought he'd get him a horn for about $10 to $15, you know. So Frank picked out the best horn. The man told him about $35 or $40, $50. He said, what, for what? He said, I wouldn't pay that for Gable's horn.
That's why he's got a Gable.

That's like we played the Boston club, one was New Year's Eve night, and one of them big guys come, the only ship, the ship line out there, he came in the club and he had something wrapped up which was liquor in a bottle, see. And he come in, he was all stewed up. And he came over to the band and said, I say, stop that music. Well we looked at him, so Frank, he's, I don't pay him no mind. So he kept on, I say, stop that music. That music sounds like hell to me when I'm drunk. Stop that music. And he got right near the bass player, Alex Scott was playing the bass, and he took that bottle and he hit that bass in the side and burst that bass. So Frank said, don't worry about it, we'll talk to the president. So that John M. Parker's brother was president then, see. He said, we'll take care of it. We'll see that he'll pay you for it. So he come back and he gave him, offered for Alec $10. Well Alec was the fellow who could fix up that bass, you know, patch it up. So Alec wanted to take the 10, Frank wouldn't let him take it. He said, you can't get no bass for that, you got to get you a new bass. So he come back, offered him $20. Alec wanted that. He kept on, raised the $10 and $5 like that, and Frank kept telling him, he said, don't take it. He said, I ain't going to give you nothing. So Alec was saying, now look there, Frank, you can fix it so I'm going to even get my money for my bass. So I can take this bass and fix it up and start playing, keep playing. But sure enough, I believe the band accepted $50 at $60. So Alec passed the bass up at that night to see Alec somebody robbed him of that money. He got drunk and he threw up all that money. He wasn't there, but that's right. That's right.
That's about all I know about where he played on the shores. He'd be at carnivals, you know, and circuses.
